\chapter{Four Words on the Face}
\label{ch:te-face-words}
\hlchaptermodality{37}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name my eye, ear, nose and mouth in Telugu, and say which three the family agrees on and which one Telugu's word does not obviously match.}

Name \te{కన్ను}, \te{చెవి}, \te{ముక్కు} and \te{నోరు}; close the loop Chapter 32 left open on \te{కన్ను}; and say why \te{నోరు}, unlike the other three, shows no visible trace of the shared vāy root Tamil, Malayalam and Kannada all carry.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kannu]{\te{కన్ను} (kannu) — \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} a word you've already met once}

\label{lesson:TE-C37-kannu}



\begin{quote}
Head and hand, taught earlier, gave you your first two body words. This chapter gives you four more — starting with one this book has secretly used before.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కన్ను}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{కన్ను}} — \emph{kannu} — \textbf{eye}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{నా} \te{కన్ను}.} — \emph{nā kannu.} — \textquotedblleft{}My eye.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Three body words now, with two from that earlier lesson: \emph{tala}, \emph{ceyyi}, \emph{kannu} — and \emph{koḍuku}, \textquotedblleft{}son,\textquotedblright{} still fresh, one lesson back.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{కన్ను}} already appeared earlier, inside the \emph{cūḍu} lesson's own etymology note for \textbf{\te{చూడు}} — as proof that Tamil \emph{pār}, Kannada \emph{nōḍu}, Malayalam \emph{kāṇuka}, and Telugu \emph{cūḍu}, four completely unrelated everyday see-verbs, all sit beside the very same ancient eye-word: Telugu \emph{kannu}, Tamil \emph{kaṇ}, Kannada \emph{kaṇṇu}, Malayalam \emph{kaṇṇ}. That chapter named the word without ever teaching it. This lesson closes the loop.

Like \emph{tala} (\textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{ceyyi} (\textquotedblleft{}hand,\textquotedblright{} a cognate reshaped almost past recognition) before it, \emph{kannu} is native Dravidian, and here the whole family agrees on it plainly — no reshaping required.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nā kannu\textquotedblright{} — my eye
  \item the four sisters' shared eye — \textquotedblleft{}kannu … kaṇ … kaṇṇu … kaṇṇ\textquotedblright{}
  \item three body words — \textquotedblleft{}tala … ceyyi … kannu\textquotedblright{}
  \item son, daughter, eye — \textquotedblleft{}koḍuku … kūturu … kannu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my eye.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nā kannu}.) Which earlier lesson already used this exact word, and what did it prove? (\textbf{The \emph{cūḍu} lesson's} etymology note — that all four Dravidian sisters share one eye-root behind four unrelated see-verbs.) Name the two body words from that earlier lesson. (\textbf{\te{తల}}, \emph{tala}, and \textbf{\te{చెయ్యి}}, \emph{ceyyi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[cevi]{\te{చెవి} (cevi) — \textquotedblleft{}ear,\textquotedblright{} matching Tamil almost letter for letter}

\label{lesson:TE-C37-cevi}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Kannu} matched its cousins closely but not exactly. This word matches even more closely.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{చెవి}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{చెవి}} — \emph{cevi} — \textbf{ear}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{నా} \te{చెవి}.} — \emph{nā cevi.} — \textquotedblleft{}My ear.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{చెవి}} is native Dravidian, and it answers Tamil \textbf{\ta{செவி}} (\emph{cevi}) almost syllable for syllable — a plainer, closer match than \emph{kannu} found with Tamil \emph{kaṇ} just one lesson ago. Two body words in a row, both native, both recognizably the same family — but \textquotedblleft{}close cousin\textquotedblright{} is not \textquotedblleft{}identical twin\textquotedblright{}: each word drifts by its own amount, and \emph{cevi} simply happened to drift less.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nā cevi\textquotedblright{} — my ear
  \item the near-match — \textquotedblleft{}cevi … cevi\textquotedblright{}
  \item eye, then ear — \textquotedblleft{}kannu … cevi\textquotedblright{}
  \item daughter, then ear — \textquotedblleft{}kūturu … cevi\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my ear.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nā cevi}.) Which Dravidian cousin's word for ear matches \emph{cevi} most closely? (\textbf{Tamil} \emph{cevi} — almost syllable for syllable.) Did \emph{kannu} match its cousins that closely? (\textbf{Not quite} — one vowel apart from Tamil's \emph{kaṇ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mukku]{\te{ముక్కు} (mukku) — \textquotedblleft{}nose,\textquotedblright{} an inherited word with a second word's fingerprints on it}

\label{lesson:TE-C37-mukku}



\begin{quote}
Eye and ear both descend cleanly from their Proto-Dravidian roots. This word descends too — but not quite cleanly.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ముక్కు}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{ముక్కు}} — \emph{mukku} — \textbf{nose}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{నా} \te{ముక్కు}.} — \emph{nā mukku.} — \textquotedblleft{}My nose.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{ముక్కు}} descends from Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*mūnk(k)u}, and it is a real cognate of Kannada \emph{mūgu}, Malayalam \emph{mūkkŭ}, and Tamil \emph{mūkku}. But comparative Dravidian scholarship flags Telugu's own reflex as \textbf{irregular}: the consonant in the middle of the word is probably not a clean, regular descendant of \emph{*mūnk(k)u} alone. It looks contaminated by a separate Dravidian root, \textbf{*mok-}, \textquotedblleft{}face\textquotedblright{} — as if two related words leaned on each other and left a mark. \emph{Cevi} showed a word that drifted very little; \emph{mukku} shows one that drifted in a specific, traceable way, nudged by its neighbour.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nā mukku\textquotedblright{} — my nose
  \item the cousins — \textquotedblleft{}mukku … mūgu … mūkkŭ … mūkku\textquotedblright{}
  \item three body words so far — \textquotedblleft{}kannu … cevi … mukku\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}my nose.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nā mukku}.) Is \emph{mukku} a regular or an irregular reflex of its Proto-Dravidian root? (\textbf{Irregular} — likely contaminated by the separate root \emph{*mok-}, \textquotedblleft{}face.\textquotedblright{}) Which two body words so far were plain, regular matches with their cousins? (\textbf{\te{కన్ను}} and \textbf{\te{చెవి}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nōru]{\te{నోరు} (nōru) — \textquotedblleft{}mouth,\textquotedblright{} the word that breaks the chapter's pattern}

\label{lesson:TE-C37-noru}



\begin{quote}
Eye, ear, nose — three native words, three visible matches with the family, one plainer than the next. The fourth face word does not keep that streak going.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{నోరు}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{నోరు}} — \emph{nōru} — \textbf{mouth}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{నా} \te{నోరు}.} — \emph{nā nōru.} — \textquotedblleft{}My mouth.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Four body words done: \emph{kannu}, \emph{cevi}, \emph{mukku}, \emph{nōru}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Tamil and Malayalam both say \textbf{\ta{வாய்}}/\textbf{vāyi} (\emph{vāy}), \textquotedblleft{}mouth,\textquotedblright{} and Kannada's \textbf{\ka{ಬಾಯಿ}} (\emph{bāyi}) answers it through a regular sound law that turns a Tamil word-initial \emph{v-} into Kannada \emph{b-}. Three sisters, one shared root, one visible law.

\textbf{\te{నోరు}} does not obviously belong to that set. It shows no trace of \emph{vāy}, and no source consulted here states what its own deeper Proto-Dravidian root actually is — so nothing is invented for it, the same discipline applied earlier to \emph{veḷḷu}'s own unresolved history. After three straight matches — \emph{kannu} plain, \emph{cevi} nearly exact, \emph{mukku} traceably contaminated but still clearly related — \emph{nōru} is the one face word where this book cannot show you the family resemblance, only note honestly that it is not there to show.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nā nōru\textquotedblright{} — my mouth
  \item the shared root Telugu sits outside of — \textquotedblleft{}vāy … bāyi … nōru\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four face words — \textquotedblleft{}kannu … cevi … mukku … nōru\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name all four face words. (\textbf{\te{కన్ను}, \te{చెవి}, \te{ముక్కు}, \te{నోరు}}.) Which three Dravidian sisters share one root and one sound law for \textquotedblleft{}mouth,\textquotedblright{} and does Telugu's word visibly belong with them? (\textbf{Tamil, Malayalam, and Kannada}, on \emph{vāy}; \textbf{no} — \emph{nōru} shows no trace of it, and its own root is not confirmed by any source consulted here.)
\end{tcolorbox}
